summary.one_liner: Unleash is an open-source feature flag management platform that lets teams roll out, test, and control features without redeploying code.
keywords: turn features on and off without deploying
summary.what_it_does: Unleash is a feature management server with a web UI for creating and managing feature flags across environments, applications, and services. Flags can be enabled or disabled for specific users or segments using activation strategies, which means changes do not require redeploying the application. The README describes support for gradual rollouts, canary releases, kill switches, and A/B testing, plus tags for organizing flags. It offers an API-first design and integrations with Slack, Microsoft Teams, and Datadog, and it can send webhooks to other tools. Insights are provided for spotting stale flags and technical debt. Client SDKs are available for many languages, and the project can be run with Docker or as a Node.js application.
use_cases: Roll out a new feature to a percentage of users
Turn off a misbehaving feature instantly with a kill switch
Run A/B tests in a production application
Self-host a feature flag service on your own infrastructure
Deploy code to production without releasing features to users
Track and clean up stale feature flags
how_to_run: Open localhost:4242 in a browser and log in with username admin and password unleash4all
stack: Unleash client SDKs (Go, Java, Node.js, PHP, Python, Ruby, Rust, .NET, Android, Flutter, iOS, JavaScript, React, Svelte, Vue)
notable: Open-source server with a web UI and a docker compose setup for local use
Official SDKs for many backend and frontend languages, plus community SDKs
Unleash Edge is a separate component that scales frontend clients without loading the main server
Privacy-focused design where end-user data stays in the application
API-first, so most actions can be automated
caveats: Several features such as RBAC, SSO, more environments, and advanced segmentation are listed as Pro or Enterprise plan features
The default open-source setup uses publicly known demo credentials and API tokens that the README labels as insecure, so they must be changed for production
Production deployment requires a persistent server; the README points to separate guides for hosting
